os.title: OS functions and services
os.text:
OS functions and services
Understand the idea
An operating system is the main software that helps users and programs use computer hardware.
For example, it gives a program memory and helps it read a file.


What is an OS?
An operating system (OS) manages computer hardware and provides services for programs and users.


Functions of an OS
Process management: It creates and ends processes, gives them CPU time and helps them share resources safely.
Memory management: It allocates RAM, frees unused memory and stops one process from accessing another process’s private memory.
File management: It creates, reads, writes and deletes files. It also organizes folders and checks access permissions.
Device and storage management: It controls devices through drivers, manages disk space and handles input/output requests.
Other services: It detects errors, protects the system and records resource use. For example, opening a file needs the OS to check permissions and read data from storage.

types.title: Time sharing and multiprocessing
types.text:
Time sharing and multiprocessing
Understand the idea
Time sharing gives programs short turns on a CPU.
Multiprocessing uses more than one CPU or core to do work at the same time.


A. Time-sharing OS
Time-sharing OS: The CPU gives each ready process a short turn called a time slice. Fast switching lets several users or programs work interactively.
How it works: A timer can interrupt the running process. The OS saves its state and runs another process. This gives quick responses but adds switching overhead.


B. Multiprocessing OS
Two or more processors or cores run tasks at the same time.
This can improve speed and total work completed.


Types of multiprocessing
Symmetric multiprocessing (SMP): All processors are peers. Each can run OS work and user programs, and they share main memory.
Asymmetric multiprocessing (AMP): A main processor controls work, or different processors have fixed jobs. This is simpler to organize but can depend heavily on the main processor.


Key difference
Time sharing divides CPU time; multiprocessing uses multiple CPUs or cores. A modern computer can use both.
Multicore means several cores on one chip; those cores can operate as an SMP system.

process.title: Process management
process.text:
Process management
Understand the idea
A process is a program that is running.
The OS keeps track of it, gives it CPU time and releases its resources when it finishes.


What is process management?
A process is a program that is currently running.
Process management is the OS work needed to control processes and their resources.


Tasks involved
Create and end processes: The OS assigns a process ID, gives the process resources and releases those resources when it ends.
Schedule the CPU: It keeps lists of ready and waiting processes and chooses which ready process runs next.
Track and switch processes: The Process Control Block (PCB) stores the process state, registers and other details. During a context switch, the OS saves one process and restores another.
Support communication and synchronization: Processes exchange data through shared memory or messages. Locks and semaphores help protect shared data.
Handle resource problems: The OS protects processes from one another and can use policies to prevent, avoid, detect or recover from deadlocks.

ipc.title: IPC and the process control block
ipc.text:
IPC and the process control block
Understand the idea
Processes sometimes need to exchange data.
Interprocess communication (IPC) provides ways to do this. A process control block (PCB) stores the information the OS needs to manage one process.


What is IPC?
Interprocess communication (IPC) allows processes to exchange data and coordinate their work.
Its two main models are shared memory and message passing.


Model 1: Shared memory
Shared memory: The OS creates a memory region that two or more processes can access. They exchange data by reading and writing this region.
Shared-memory example: A producer puts items in a shared buffer and a consumer removes them. A mutex or semaphore prevents unsafe access.


Model 2: Message passing
Message passing: Processes communicate using send and receive operations. The OS manages the communication channel, such as a pipe or message queue.
Message-passing options: Messages may go directly to a process or through a mailbox. Sending and receiving can block until ready, or return without waiting.


Main difference
Shared memory is efficient for large amounts of data but needs careful synchronization.
Message passing keeps processes more separate and can work across machines, but copying messages and OS calls may add overhead.

distributed.title: Distributed operating systems
distributed.text:
Distributed operating systems
Understand the idea
A distributed system uses several connected computers to share work. A distributed operating system helps manage their resources together.


Meaning
A distributed OS coordinates several connected computers and tries to make their resources work like one system.
Each computer has its own CPU and memory.


Uses
It supports shared storage, distributed computation and services spread across several machines.


Features
Resource sharing: access devices, files and services on other computers.
Load sharing: distribute work between computers.
Transparency: hide where a resource is located.
Communication: nodes coordinate through network messages.


Advantages
Greater processing capacity and shared resources.
Can grow by adding computers.
Redundant services can continue after some failures.


Disadvantages
Network delays and partial failures.
Difficult data consistency, security and coordination.

spool.title: Spooling and buffering
spool.text:
Spooling and buffering
Understand the idea
Spooling stores complete jobs in a waiting area, such as documents waiting for a printer.
Buffering temporarily holds data while it moves between parts that work at different speeds.


A. Spooling
Spooling: Complete jobs wait in a queue, usually on disk, for a shared device or service.
Spooling example: Several programs submit print jobs. The print spooler sends them to the printer one at a time.


B. Buffering
Buffering: Data is temporarily kept in a buffer while moving between a producer and a consumer. Buffers are usually held in RAM.
Why buffering is needed: Devices work at different speeds. A buffer lets a faster producer continue for a while without waiting for every slow transfer.
Buffering example: A keyboard buffer holds typed characters until the program reads them. Double buffering lets one buffer fill while the other is processed.


Main difference
Buffering smooths a data transfer; spooling queues jobs.
Both let work overlap with slow I/O, but they need storage and queue management.

terms.title: Synchronization vocabulary
terms.text:
Synchronization vocabulary
Understand the idea
When programs share data, their actions must be coordinated.
Otherwise, two programs may change the same value in the wrong order.


Semaphore
A synchronization tool with an integer count.
Atomic wait() takes a permit or blocks; signal() returns a permit and may wake a waiting process. A counting semaphore can manage several resource instances.


Mutual exclusion (only one process enters at a time)
Only one process at a time can enter a section of code that protects shared data.


Race condition
The result changes depending on the order in which processes run. For example, two processes may both read counter = 5 and both write 6, losing one increment.


Critical section
The part of a program that accesses shared data. Its structure is: entry section → critical section → exit section → remaining code.


Deadlock
Processes wait forever for resources held by one another.
Example: P1 holds A and waits for B, while P2 holds B and waits for A.

memory.title: Need for memory management
memory.text:
Need for memory management
Understand the idea
Memory management decides which program gets which part of RAM.
It also protects programs from changing one another’s memory.


What is memory management?
Memory management is the OS function that tracks and controls how main memory (RAM) is used.


Why it is needed
Keep track of space: The OS records which memory areas are free and which belong to each process.
Allocate and free memory: It gives memory to programs when needed and takes it back when they finish.
Protect processes: It stops a program from reading or changing memory that it is not allowed to access.
Translate addresses and allow sharing: It maps a program’s logical addresses to physical RAM and allows controlled sharing of code or data.
Use memory efficiently: It tries to reduce wasted space and manages problems such as fragmentation.
Support virtual memory: It can keep only the needed pages in RAM and load other pages later. This improves flexibility, but too many page faults make the system slow.

disk.title: Disk structure and performance
disk.text:
Disk structure and performance
Understand the idea
A magnetic disk stores data on rotating surfaces.
Reading a block takes time to move the head, wait for the block and transfer the data.


A. Disk structure
Structure: A hard disk has rotating platters. Each surface contains circular tracks, and each track is divided into sectors.
Heads and cylinders: Read/write heads access the surfaces. A cylinder is the set of tracks at the same radius on all surfaces. An actuator moves the heads.


B. Disk performance
Seek time: Time needed to move the head to the correct track.
Rotational delay: Time spent waiting for the required sector to rotate under the head. On average, this is about half a rotation.
Transfer time: Time taken to read or write the data after the head is in position. Access time ≈ seek time + rotational delay + transfer time, plus other overhead.


Example: 7200 RPM
At 7200 RPM, one rotation takes 60/7200 = 8.33 ms. Average rotational delay is about 4.17 ms. This is an example, not a value given in the paper.


Performance factors
Sequential access usually needs less head movement than random access.
Caching and scheduling can help. SSDs have no moving heads, so seek and rotation delays do not apply to them.

The way a user interacts with the computer.

schedule.title: SSTF and SCAN comparison
schedule.text:
SSTF and SCAN comparison
Understand the idea
SSTF serves the nearest request first. SCAN serves requests along one direction of travel and then reverses at the disk boundary.


A. SSTF
SSTF meaning: Shortest Seek Time First chooses the pending request closest to the current head position.
SSTF advantage: It often reduces average head movement compared with serving requests in arrival order.
SSTF disadvantage: Far-away requests may wait a long time if nearby requests keep arriving. It does not always give the shortest total route.


B. SCAN
SCAN meaning: The head moves toward one disk boundary, serving requests in order, then reverses. It works like an elevator.
SCAN advantage: It gives more predictable service than SSTF because requests are served on repeated sweeps.
SCAN disadvantage: The head may travel to a boundary even when no request is there. A request just behind the head may wait for the return sweep.


Numerical requirements
State the starting head position, direction and cylinder limits. SCAN goes to a boundary; LOOK turns at the last pending request.
Head movement and seek time are different quantities.

virtual.text:
Disk management and virtual memory
Understand the idea
Virtual memory lets a program use an address space without keeping all of it in RAM at once.
Disk management organizes the storage used by files and other data.


A. Disk management
Disk management: The OS organizes and maintains storage so that files can be saved and retrieved reliably.
Main disk tasks: Create partitions, format a file system, track free blocks and allocate blocks to files. Device controllers may detect and remap damaged sectors.


B. Virtual memory
Virtual memory: A process uses virtual addresses that the OS and hardware map to physical RAM. Not every page needs to remain in RAM all the time.
Working: The page table records where pages are located and whether they are present. Accessing a valid but absent page causes a page fault.
Page-fault handling: The OS obtains a frame, loads the page from backing storage, updates the mapping and retries the instruction. A changed victim page may need to be saved first.
Benefits: Better memory use, process isolation and support for larger address spaces. Costs include page-table storage and slow page faults; too many faults can cause thrashing.

ostypes.text:
OS types and services
Understand the idea
Different operating systems are designed for different needs, such as handling batches of work, giving quick responses or using several processors.


A. Types of operating systems
Batch OS: Runs collected jobs with little user interaction. Multiprogramming OS: keeps several jobs in memory so the CPU can work while another job waits for I/O.
Time-sharing OS: Gives users or programs short CPU turns for quick responses. Multiprocessing OS: uses several CPUs or cores at once.
Other types: A real-time OS works with timing limits. A network OS provides services across separate machines. A distributed OS tries to coordinate connected machines as one system. These categories can overlap.


B. Services provided by an OS
Program and I/O services: The OS loads and runs programs and provides controlled access to input/output devices.
File and communication services: It manages files and directories and lets processes exchange data through shared memory or messages.
Resource services: It allocates CPU time, memory and devices. It also records resource use.
Protection and errors: It checks permissions, isolates processes and detects faults. Programs request these services through system calls; for example, reading a file asks the OS to check access and retrieve data.

deadlock.title: Deadlock conditions and prevention
deadlock.text:
Deadlock conditions and prevention
Understand the idea
Deadlock occurs when processes wait for resources held by one another, so none of them can continue.


A. Why deadlock occurs
Deadlock means processes wait forever for resources held by one another.
It can occur when all four conditions below hold.
Mutual exclusion (only one process enters at a time): a resource can be used by only one process at a time.
Hold and wait: a process keeps a resource while requesting another.
No preemption: a resource cannot be taken away forcibly.
Circular wait: processes form a cycle, each waiting for the next.


B. Prevention techniques
Break mutual exclusion (only one process enters at a time): Make a resource shareable where safe. This cannot be done for every resource, such as data that must be changed by only one process at a time.
Break hold and wait: Ask for all required resources together, or release held resources before asking for new ones. This can waste resources or delay work.
Break no preemption: Take a resource back when its state can be safely saved and restored. This is not suitable for every device or operation.
Break circular wait: Give resources a fixed order and need every process to request them in that order. This stops a cycle of waiting.

critical.title: Requirements of a critical-section solution
critical.text:
Requirements of a critical-section solution
Understand the idea
A critical section is the part of a program that accesses shared data. A correct solution must control entry without making processes wait unfairly.


Critical section
A critical section is code that accesses shared data. A correct solution must protect this code when several processes run together.


Three requirements
Mutual exclusion (only one process enters at a time): Only one process can be inside the protected critical section at a time.
Progress: If the section is free and processes want to enter, choosing the next process must not be delayed forever. Processes doing unrelated work must not stop that choice.
Bounded waiting: After a process asks to enter, there must be a limit on how many times others can enter before it. This prevents starvation (waiting indefinitely while others are served).


Example
Example: Two processes read counter = 5 and both write 6. One increment is lost. Protect the full read–change–write operation with a suitable lock.
Program structure: Entry section → Critical section → Exit section → Remaining code. Example: lock(m); counter = counter + 1; unlock(m).


Implementation note
Lock operations must be atomic. A lock’s fairness depends on its implementation; mutual exclusion (only one process enters at a time) alone does not guarantee bounded waiting.

When the page is present: The CPU uses the frame number and the offset to form the physical address.
When a valid page is absent: A page fault occurs. The OS finds a free frame or chooses a victim, saves the victim if necessary, loads the required page and updates the table.
Restart: The OS retries the instruction that caused the fault. An invalid address is treated as an error, not as a page to load.

fit.title: Dynamic memory allocation algorithms
fit.text:

Understand the idea
Memory allocation chooses a free block for a request.
First fit, best fit and worst fit differ in how they select that block.


Purpose
These algorithms choose a free memory hole for a process that needs one continuous block.
If the hole is larger than required, the unused part remains free.


First fit
Select the first hole large enough.
It is usually quick because searching stops early, but small holes may collect near the start.


Best fit
Select the smallest hole large enough.
It leaves the smallest immediate remainder, but may create tiny holes and needs more searching.


Worst fit
Select the largest hole.
It leaves a larger remainder, but uses up the biggest free regions and may need a full search.


Worked example
Holes: 100, 500, 200, 300, 600 KB.
Request: 212 KB.
Each method starts with the original holes.

reliability.title: Disk reliability and stable storage
reliability.text:
Disk reliability and stable storage
Understand the idea
Reliable storage aims to keep data available despite failures.
Backups, extra copies and checks help reduce the risk of losing data.


A. Disk reliability
Disk reliability: The ability to store and retrieve correct data despite faults such as bad sectors, hardware failure or power loss.
Protection methods: Error-detecting/correcting codes, bad-block remapping, device monitoring and backups help protect data.
Redundancy: Mirroring keeps copies on different disks. Parity-based schemes can rebuild data after certain failures. Redundancy does not replace backups because deletion or corruption can affect live copies.


B. Stable storage
Stable storage: An ideal model in which saved data survives failures. Real systems approximate it with independent copies and careful writing/recovery rules.
Example write method: Write and confirm copy A first, then write and confirm copy B. After a crash, use checksums and version information to find a valid current copy and repair the other.


Recovery and limits
Crash recovery: A journal or write-ahead log records changes so the file system can recover a consistent state. Data must be flushed through caches when durability is required.
Limitation: Guarantees depend on assumptions about failures and atomic writes. No finite system protects against every possible failure.

scan24.text:
SSTF and SCAN: the end-sem numerical
Understand the idea
SSTF chooses the closest waiting disk request. SCAN moves in one direction towards a boundary and then reverses.
Their paths can give different total distances.


Given data
Requests = 98, 183, 37, 122, 14, 124, 65, 67. Starting head = 53.


A. SSTF
SSTF route: Choose the closest pending request each time. Route: 53 → 65 → 67 → 37 → 14 → 98 → 122 → 124 → 183.
SSTF movement: 12 + 2 + 30 + 23 + 84 + 24 + 2 + 59 = 236 cylinders.


B. SCAN: assumptions
The paper gives neither the initial direction nor the disk limits.
Assume cylinders 0–199 and a downward initial direction.


SCAN moving downward
53 → 37 → 14 → 0 → 65 → 67 → 98 → 122 → 124 → 183. Movement until the last request = 53 + 183 = 236 cylinders.


Alternative: SCAN moving upward
Route goes to 199 before returning to 37 and 14. Movement = (199 − 53) + (199 − 14) = 331 cylinders.


Units
Both SCAN totals depend on the stated assumptions.
The paper asks for seek time, but no timing model is supplied.
Report head movement in cylinders, not milliseconds.

access.title: Three file access methods
access.text:
Three file access methods
Understand the idea
A file access method describes how a program reads or writes records: in order, at a chosen position, or through an index.


Sequential access
Sequential access: Read or write records in order, using a current position in the file. It suits text streams and logs.
Sequential tradeoff: It is simple for processing the whole file, but finding a later record may need reading or skipping earlier records.


Direct access
Direct access: Move to a chosen block or byte offset and read or write there. It suits databases and large binary files.
Direct example: With fixed-size records, a record number can be converted into an offset. Variable-size records need extra information to locate them.


Indexed access
Indexed access: Use an index that maps a key or record number to its location. Example: look up a student’s roll number and then read that student’s record.
Indexed tradeoff: Finding records is faster, and ordered indexes can help with ranges. However, the index needs space and must be updated when records change.

directory.title: Three directory structures
directory.text:
Three directory structures
Understand the idea
A directory stores file names and information needed to find files.
Directory structures organize files into simple lists or groups of folders.


Directory
A directory connects file names to file information or identifiers.
It helps users find and organize files.


Single-level directory
All files are kept in one directory.
It is simple, but names can clash and large collections are difficult to organize.


Two-level directory
Two-level directory: A main directory contains a separate directory for each user. Different users can use the same file name.
Two-level limitation: A user still has limited grouping within one directory, and sharing between users needs extra support.


Tree-structured directory
Tree structure: Directories can contain files and subdirectories. A root directory is at the top. This supports clear grouping and larger collections.
Paths: An absolute path starts from the root; a relative path starts from the current directory. For example, /students/notes/os.txt and /staff/notes/os.txt can both exist.

android.title: Android file-system working
android.text:
Android file-system working
Understand the idea
Android uses file systems to store system files and app data.
Each app normally has a private area, while shared storage follows access rules.


File-system structure
Basic idea: Android uses the Linux kernel and a folder-based file system. The storage format can vary by device; ext4 and F2FS are examples.
Storage areas: Some areas hold the system, some hold private app data and others hold shared user content.


App isolation and access
App protection: Apps normally have separate Linux user IDs. Permissions and security policies help stop one app from reading another app’s private files.
Private and shared files: An app uses app-specific storage for its own data. Shared media and user-selected documents are accessed through suitable platform APIs, such as MediaStore or the Storage Access Framework.
Scoped storage: Modern Android limits broad access to shared storage. “External storage” is a logical storage category; it does not always mean a removable SD card.


How a file is written
The app requests a write through a file API.
The kernel checks access and passes the request through its file-system layer.
The underlying file system finds the storage blocks and writes the data.

pcb_ipc.title: PCB and interprocess communication
pcb_ipc.text:
PCB and interprocess communication
Understand the idea
Processes sometimes need to exchange data.
Interprocess communication (IPC) provides ways to do this. A process control block (PCB) stores the information the OS needs to manage one process.


A. Process Control Block (PCB)
The Process Control Block (PCB) is the OS record for one process. It contains the information needed to manage and resume that process.
PCB contents: Process ID, current state, program counter, CPU registers, priority, memory information, open files and accounting details.
Context switching: The OS saves the running process’s CPU state and restores the next process’s state using its PCB and related structures. The PCB is not the whole program memory.


B. Interprocess communication (IPC)
IPC meaning: Interprocess communication lets processes exchange data and coordinate work.
Shared memory: Processes read and write a common region. It is efficient for large data, but locks or semaphores are needed to prevent races.
Message passing: Processes use send and receive operations through channels such as pipes or queues. It keeps data more separate and can work across machines, but may add copying overhead.
Example: A producer and consumer can share a protected buffer, or send items through a message queue.

multiprocessing.title: Multiprocessing, SMP and multicore
multiprocessing.text:
Multiprocessing, SMP and multicore
Understand the idea
Time sharing gives programs short turns on a CPU.
Multiprocessing uses more than one CPU or core to do work at the same time.


A. Multiprocessing OS
Multiprocessing means using two or more processors or cores to run work at the same time. The OS schedules tasks across them.
Benefits: More tasks can finish in a given time. Parallel programs may run faster, and sharing resources can reduce overall cost.


B. Symmetric multiprocessing
Processors are peers, share main memory and can run OS tasks and user programs.


C. Multicore system
Multicore: A single processor chip contains several processing cores. Cores may share caches and main memory.
Relationship: SMP describes how processors are organized; multicore describes the hardware. A multicore computer can use SMP.


Challenges
The OS must balance work and protect shared data.
Shared memory or cache access can become a bottleneck.

paging_hardware.title: Paging hardware
paging_hardware.text:
Paging hardware
Understand the idea
Paging divides a program’s memory into equal-sized pages and RAM into equal-sized frames. A page table tells us which frame holds each page.


Address format
page number and offset.
Pages and physical memory frames have the same size.


Hardware components
The Memory Management Unit (MMU) translates this address. It uses the page number to find a frame number in the process’s page table.
A page-table entry stores the frame number and control bits, such as presence and access rights. A page-table base register identifies where the table is stored.
The Translation Lookaside Buffer (TLB) is a small fast cache of recent translations. A hit supplies the frame quickly; a miss needs looking up the page table.


Address translation
The physical address is frame number × page size + offset.
The offset does not change during translation.


Page fault vs TLB miss
If a legal page is absent, a page fault transfers control to the OS to load it.
An invalid access causes an error. A TLB miss alone is not a page fault.

distributed_spool.title: Distributed OS and spooling
distributed_spool.text:
Distributed OS and spooling
Understand the idea
A distributed system uses several connected computers to share work. A distributed operating system helps manage their resources together.


Distributed OS
Distributed OS: An OS that coordinates several networked computers and aims to offer a unified view of their resources.
Working: Each computer has its own CPU and memory. Computers exchange messages to share resources and distribute tasks.
Benefits and limits: It can share work and grow by adding nodes, but network delays, partial failures and consistency make coordination difficult.


Spooling
Spooling: Keeping jobs in a queue, usually on disk, until a shared device or service can process them.
Example: Programs submit print jobs to a queue. The spooler sends each job to the printer in turn.
Benefit: The program can continue after submitting its job instead of waiting for the whole print operation. Spooling still needs storage and queue management.
